Community change at stated time lags (temporal variogram)

Source: R/AllGenerics.R, R/getVariogram.R
getVariogram.Rd

Estimates \(D(L)\), the expected dissimilarity between two samples of the same subject taken \(L\) time units apart, from all within-subject sample pairs. Unlike divergence to the previous sample, \(D(L)\) refers to a stated lag, so it can be compared between subjects, groups and studies whose sampling schedules differ.

getVariogram(x, ...)

addVariogram(x, ...)

# S4 method for class 'SummarizedExperiment'
addVariogram(x, name = "variogram", ...)

# S4 method for class 'SummarizedExperiment'
getVariogram(
  x,
  time.col,
  group,
  assay.type = "counts",
  method = "bray",
  time.lag = NULL,
  split.by = NULL,
  time.point = NULL,
  window = 2,
  squared = FALSE,
  conf.level = 0.95,
  ...
)

Arguments

x

A SummarizedExperiment object.

...

additional arguments passed to getDissimilarity().

name

Character scalar. Specifies a name for storing the results in metadata. (Default: "variogram")

time.col

Character scalar. Specifies a name of the column from colData that identifies the sampling time points for the samples.

group

Character scalar. Specifies a name of the column from colData that identifies the subject (or other unit followed over time) of each sample. Pairs are formed within subjects.

assay.type

Character scalar. Specifies which assay values are used in the dissimilarity estimation. (Default: "counts")

method

Character scalar. Used to calculate the dissimilarity Method is passed to the function that is specified by dis.fun. (Default: "bray")

time.lag

NULL or numeric vector. The lags \(L\), in the units of time.col, at which \(D(L)\) is estimated. If NULL, ten lags between the shortest and longest supported lag. (Default: NULL)

split.by

NULL or Character scalar. Specifies a name of a column from colData with one value per subject. \(D(L)\) is estimated for each of its levels, and each level is compared with the first. (Default: NULL)

time.point

NULL, numeric vector or "median". The time at which \(D(L)\) is estimated, for communities whose change depends on time since a common origin; one value, or one per lag. See details. (Default: NULL)

window

Numeric scalar. Pairs with lags within a factor of window of \(L\) are used. (Default: 2)

squared

Logical scalar. Whether the dissimilarities are squared. (Default: FALSE)

conf.level

Numeric scalar. Confidence level of the intervals. (Default: 0.95)

Value

getVariogram returns a DataFrame with one row per lag (and level of split.by, and comparison) and the columns

lag

The lag \(L\).

split.by

When split.by is given: the level, or the comparison ("B / A").

type

"dissimilarity" for estimates of \(D(L)\), "ratio" for comparisons between levels.

estimate, lower, upper

\(D(L)\) or the ratio of \(D(L)\), with the confidence interval.

se

Standard error on the log scale.

df

Degrees of freedom of the t distribution.

p.value

For comparisons, the p-value of the test that the ratio is 1.

n.subjects, n.pairs

Subjects and pairs in the lag window.

supported

Whether the design supports \(D(L)\) at this lag.

time.point

The time at which \(D(L)\) was estimated, when time.point is given.

addVariogram returns x with this table in its metadata.

Details

Every pair of samples from the same subject measures how much the community changed over that pair's time lag \(h\). The temporal variogram \(g(h)\) is the expected dissimilarity as a function of the lag, and \(D(L) = g(L)\). Divergence to the previous sample measures change at whatever intervals the schedule happens to have, so it differs between designs even when the dynamics are the same.

\(D(L)\) is estimated locally. Pairs with lags in \([L / window, L \times window]\) are used, and the dissimilarities are regressed on \(u = \log(h / L)\) and \(u^2\) by weighted least squares; the intercept estimates \(D(L)\). The pairs of each subject are weighted so that every subject counts equally. Pairs of the same subject share samples and are correlated, so the standard error is cluster-robust by subject (CR1), and the interval for \(\log D(L)\) uses a t distribution with \(G - 1\) degrees of freedom, where \(G\) is the number of subjects with pairs in the window.

\(D(L)\) is reported only at lags the design supports: at least \(\max(5, 20\%)\) of the subjects with two or more samples must have pairs in the window, and at least three subjects must have pairs at lags up to \(L\) and three at lags from \(L\), so that \(D(L)\) is interpolated, not extrapolated. The window must also contain at least twice as many subjects as regression coefficients (6, or 10 with time.point), because the sandwich variance is singular when there are as many subjects as coefficients. Elsewhere the estimate is NA and supported is FALSE.

When time.lag = NULL, ten lags are spread evenly on the log scale between the shortest and longest supported lag of the whole data: the smallest and largest lag reached by at least \(\max(5, 20\%)\) of the subjects.

Groups. With split.by, \(D(L)\) is estimated separately for each level of a subject-level variable, and each level is compared with the first level by the ratio of \(D(L)\), with a Welch–Satterthwaite t test of the log ratio. The comparison is made only at lags supported in both groups. P-values are not adjusted for multiple comparisons.

Developing communities. When change at a given lag depends on the time since a common origin (age in infant cohorts, time since an intervention), groups whose samples were taken at different ages differ in \(D(L)\) even with the same development. time.point estimates \(D(L)\) at a stated time \(a\): only pairs whose midpoint \(m\) satisfies \((1 + m) / (1 + a)\) in \([1/2, 2]\) are used, the regression adds \(z = \log(1 + m) - \log(1 + a)\) and \(z^2\), and at least three subjects must have midpoints up to \(a\) and three from \(a\). With time.point = "median", \(a\) is the median midpoint of all pairs in the lag window, pooled over the levels of split.by, so that every group is evaluated at the same time. Time must then be measured from the common origin and be non-negative.

Dissimilarity. Any dissimilarity of getDissimilarity() can be used. The squared Euclidean distance between Hellinger-transformed abundances (method = "euclidean", squared = TRUE on a "hellinger" assay) adds technical noise to the dissimilarity additively, so the noise does not change the shape of the variogram, only its level. Dissimilarities depend on sequencing depth; rarefy the counts first (rarefyAssay()) when depth differs between samples or groups.

References

Diggle P.J. (1988) An approach to the analysis of repeated measurements. Biometrics 44, 959–971. doi: 10.2307/2531727

Lloyd-Price J., et al. (2019) Multi-omics of the gut microbial ecosystem in inflammatory bowel diseases. Nature 569, 655–662. doi: 10.1038/s41586-019-1237-9

Björk J.R., et al. (2022) Synchrony and idiosyncrasy in the gut microbiome of wild baboons. Nature Ecology & Evolution 6, 955–964. doi: 10.1038/s41559-022-01773-4

See also

getStepwiseDivergence()

Examples

library(miaTime)

data(hitchip1006)
tse <- transformAssay(hitchip1006, method = "hellinger")

# Change over 1 to 9 time units, as squared Hellinger distance
res <- getVariogram(
    tse,
    time.col = "time",
    group = "subject",
    assay.type = "hellinger",
    method = "euclidean",
    squared = TRUE,
    time.lag = c(1, 3, 6, 9)
    )
res
#> DataFrame with 4 rows and 11 columns
#>         lag          type  estimate     lower     upper        se        df
#>   <numeric>   <character> <numeric> <numeric> <numeric> <numeric> <numeric>
#> 1         1 dissimilarity        NA        NA        NA        NA        NA

#> 3         6 dissimilarity  0.233434  0.184348  0.295591 0.1175358        50
#> 4         9 dissimilarity  0.136988  0.113095  0.165930 0.0926525        23
#>     p.value n.subjects   n.pairs supported
#>   <numeric>  <integer> <integer> <logical>
#> 1        NA         15        88     FALSE
#> 2        NA         59        73      TRUE
#> 3        NA         51        73      TRUE
#> 4        NA         24        46      TRUE

# Compare the sexes
res <- getVariogram(
    tse,
    time.col = "time",
    group = "subject",
    assay.type = "hellinger",
    method = "euclidean",
    squared = TRUE,
    time.lag = c(1, 3),
    split.by = "sex"
    )
#> 37 samples with missing values in 'time', 'subject' or 'sex' were removed.
res[res$type == "ratio", ]
